Arkansas Attorney General Sues Sweepstakes Casino Operator VGW

Published November 7, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Arkansas Attorney General Tim Griffin has filed suit against VGW, the Australian company behind the Chumba Casino, LuckyLand, and Global Poker sweepstakes platforms, alleging its dual-currency model violates the state's Deceptive Trade Practices Act.

The argument: this is gambling, whatever it's called

Griffin's office argues VGW's claim that it isn't a gambling business doesn't hold up. "Arkansas's gambling laws are clear," Griffin said, adding that any company "providing a means for Arkansans to gamble money within our state" is subject to the same rules that govern legal gambling. VGW's platforms run on a model common across the sweepstakes-casino industry: players buy a virtual currency to play slot-style and table games, and separately receive a second, non-purchasable currency that can be redeemed for cash prizes. Griffin called the distinction between the two currencies "weak at best," arguing courts have repeatedly rejected that same "too-cute-by-half" logic from other operators. The suit seeks restitution, penalties, back taxes, and an injunction against VGW's Arkansas operations; no specific dollar figure was disclosed. Griffin's office filed a similar suit against prediction-market operator Kalshi around the same time.

Arkansas joins a growing list of states

Real-money online casino gaming is not legal in Arkansas, though sports betting is, and the legislature has previously considered — but not passed — bills that would have explicitly banned dual-currency sweepstakes casinos or created a licensed online casino framework instead. This isn't VGW's first brush with a state regulator this year: in September, New York Attorney General Letitia James secured an $8 million settlement from the company over the same Chumba, Global Poker, and LuckyLand platforms. Eight states — California, Connecticut, Indiana, Maine, Montana, Nevada, New Jersey, and New York — have now passed laws banning sweepstakes casinos outright, and VGW has reportedly received cease-and-desist notices in others.

A company already in transition

The Arkansas suit lands as VGW works through its own internal changes. LuckyLand Slots was announced in September to be permanently closing in North America, and the company has been led by interim chief Mats Johnson since February, after founder Laurence Escalante formally stepped down in July. For Arkansas players, the suit doesn't change VGW's platforms' availability today, but it adds the state to a rapidly expanding patchwork of sweepstakes-casino enforcement that bettors should watch before assuming any dual-currency site is settled law in their state.
